reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / DeVita's Cancer: Principles & Practice of Oncology
clinicalPearls: Asbestos exposure is the dominant cause, with a characteristically long latency of several decades between exposure and disease onset
The pleura is the most common site, presenting with breathlessness and chest pain, often accompanied by a unilateral pleural effusion; the peritoneum is a less common site
A detailed occupational and environmental exposure history is essential, since exposure may have been remote, indirect, or through household contact
Pleural fluid cytology alone is often insufficient, and definitive diagnosis usually requires tissue biopsy, best obtained by thoracoscopy with immunohistochemical confirmation
The epithelioid subtype carries a better prognosis than the sarcomatoid or biphasic subtypes, which are more aggressive
The disease tends to spread by local extension over the pleural surfaces and encases the lung rather than forming discrete masses, making complete surgical clearance difficult
Management is usually multimodal and largely palliative, combining platinum-based chemotherapy, increasingly with immunotherapy, alongside radiotherapy and surgery in selected fit patients
Effusion control with pleurodesis or an indwelling catheter and good symptom management are central to care, and cases often carry medicolegal and compensation implications
reference.pathophysiology: Malignant mesothelioma arises from the mesothelial cells lining the pleural, peritoneal, or, rarely, pericardial cavities. Inhaled asbestos fibres, particularly amphibole types, are retained in tissues and provoke chronic inflammation, oxidative injury, and DNA damage over many years, leading to malignant transformation. The tumour characteristically grows as a diffuse rind along serosal surfaces, encasing the lung and invading the chest wall, diaphragm, and mediastinum. Histological subtypes range from epithelioid through biphasic to the more aggressive sarcomatoid form.
additionalDifferentials: Primary lung carcinoma with pleural involvement
Benign asbestos-related pleural disease and pleural plaques
Pleural lymphoma or other rare pleural tumours
additionalInvestigations: Chest radiograph and contrast-enhanced CT of the chest to assess pleural thickening and effusion
Pleural fluid aspiration for cytology, recognising its limited sensitivity
Thoracoscopic or image-guided pleural biopsy with immunohistochemistry for definitive diagnosis
MRI or PET-CT to define local extent and staging in surgical candidates
Detailed documentation of asbestos exposure history for clinical and medicolegal purposes
redFlags: Progressive breathlessness with a large or recurrent unilateral pleural effusion
Persistent chest wall pain suggesting local tumour invasion
Rapid clinical deterioration or weight loss indicating aggressive disease
Superior vena cava obstruction or extensive chest wall involvement
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally poor with limited long-term survival; the epithelioid subtype, early stage, and good performance status favour longer survival, while sarcomatoid histology and advanced disease predict rapid progression.
pitfalls: Relying on pleural fluid cytology alone and delaying tissue biopsy
Failing to elicit a remote or indirect asbestos exposure history
Overlooking the medicolegal and compensation dimensions of the diagnosis
Offering aggressive surgery to patients unlikely to benefit given subtype or stage
references: DeVita's Cancer: Principles & Practice of Oncology
management: Offer systemic therapy with platinum-pemetrexed chemotherapy, increasingly combined with immune checkpoint inhibition (nivolumab plus ipilimumab) as first-line treatment
Consider lung-preserving surgery (pleurectomy/decortication) within a multimodality plan for selected early epithelioid disease, with radiotherapy for local control or symptom palliation
Control the recurrent pleural effusion and breathlessness with indwelling pleural catheter drainage or talc pleurodesis
Provide early palliative care with opioid analgesia and neuropathic agents for chest-wall pain and breathlessness
Monitor disease with interval contrast-enhanced CT to detect progression and guide further lines of therapy
Manage through a thoracic oncology multidisciplinary team including surgery, oncology, respiratory medicine, and palliative care
Document the asbestos exposure history and advise the patient on compensation and medicolegal entitlements
